entries.2d363f551cb752d55934dfc131ccd806b5c0b46a: <div sID="gen4200" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="6" osisID="Josh.6" sID="Josh.6"/> <div eID="gen4200" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4201" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen4202" type="x-p"/> Joshua opened the campaign with the siege of Jericho, a city which could not trust so much to the courage of its people as to act offensively, and to send out its forces to oppose Israel's landing and encamping, but trusted so much to the strength of its walls as to stand upon its defence, and not to surrender, or desire conditions of peace. Now here we have the story of the taking of it, I. The directions and assurances which the captain of the Lord's host gave concerning it, <reference osisRef="Josh.6.1-Josh.6.5">ver. 1-5</reference>. II. The trial of the people's patient obedience in walking round the city six days, <reference osisRef="Josh.6.6-Josh.6.14">ver. 6-14</reference>. III. The wonderful delivery of it into their hands the seventh day, with a solemn charge to them to use it as a devoted thing, <reference osisRef="Josh.6.15-Josh.6.21">ver. 15-21</reference> and <reference osisRef="Josh.6.24">24</reference>. IV. The preservation of Rahab and her relations, <reference osisRef="Josh.6.22-Josh.6.23">ver. 22, 23</reference>, <reference osisRef="Josh.6.25">25</reference>. V. A curse pronounced upon the man that should dare to rebuild this city, <reference osisRef="Josh.6.26-Josh.6.27">ver. 26, 27</reference>. An abstract of this story we find among the trophies of faith, <reference osisRef="Heb.11.30">Heb. xi. 30</reference>. "By faith the walls of Jericho fell down, after they were compassed about seven days."
entries.2242138aa0f8d96d899641c1c4defb82f3bb6747: <div eID="gen4202" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen4201" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Siege of Jericho. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1451.)</title> <div sID="gen4203" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Now Jericho was straitly shut up because of the children of Israel: none went out, and none came in. <hi type="super">2</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> said unto Joshua, See, I have given into thine hand Jericho, and the king thereof, <hi type="italic">and</hi> the mighty men of valour. <hi type="super">3</hi> And ye shall compass the city, all <hi type="italic">ye</hi> men of war, <hi type="italic">and</hi> go round about the city once. Thus shalt thou do six days. <hi type="super">4</hi> And seven priests shall bear before the ark seven trumpets of rams' horns: and the seventh day ye shall compass the city seven times, and the priests shall blow with the trumpets. <hi type="super">5</hi> And it shall come to pass, that when they make a long <hi type="italic">blast</hi> with the ram's horn, <hi type="italic">and</hi> when ye hear the sound of the trumpet, all the people shall shout with a great shout; and the wall of the city shall fall down flat, and the people shall ascend up every man straight before him. <div eID="gen4203" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4204" type="x-p"/> We have here a contest between God and the men of Jericho, and their different resolutions, upon which it is easy to say whose word shall prevail. <div eID="gen4204" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4205" type="x-p"/> I. Jericho resolves Israel shall <hi type="italic">not</hi> be its master, <reference osisRef="Josh.6.1">v. 1</reference>. It was <hi type="italic">straitly shut up, because of the children of Israel.</hi> It <hi type="italic">did shut up, and it was shut up</hi> (so it is in the margin); it <hi type="italic">did shut up</hi> itself, being strongly fortified both by art and nature, and it <hi type="italic">was shut up</hi> by the obstinacy and resolution of the inhabitants, who agreed never to surrender nor so much as sound a parley; none went out as deserters or to treat of peace, nor were any admitted in to offer peace. Thus were they infatuated, and their hearts hardened to their own destruction—the miserable case and character of all those that <hi type="italic">strengthen themselves against the Almighty,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.15.25">Job xv. 25</reference>. <div eID="gen4205" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4206" type="x-p"/> II. God resolves Israel <hi type="italic">shall</hi> be its master, and that quickly, The captain of the Lord's host, here called <hi type="italic">Jehovah,</hi> taking notice how strongly Jericho was fortified and how strictly guarded, and knowing Joshua's thoughts and cares about reducing it, and perhaps his fears of a disgrace there and of stumbling at the threshold, gave him here all the assurance he could desire of success (<reference osisRef="Josh.6.2">v. 2</reference>): <hi type="italic">See, I have given into thy hand Jericho.</hi> Not, "<hi type="italic">I will do it,</hi> but, <hi type="italic">I have done it;</hi> it is all thy own, as sure as if it were already in thy possession." It was designed that this city, being the first-fruits of Canaan, should be entirely devoted to God, and that neither Joshua nor Israel should ever be one mite the richer for it, and yet it is here said to be <hi type="italic">given into their hand;</hi> for we must reckon that most our own which we have an opportunity of honouring God with and employing in his service. Now. 1. The captain of the Lord's host gives directions how the city should be besieged. No trenches are to be opened, no batteries erected, nor battering rams drawn up, nor any military preparations made; but the ark of God must be carried by the priests round the city once a day for six days together, and seven times the seventh day, attended by the men of war in silence, the priests all the while blowing with trumpets of rams' horns, <reference osisRef="Josh.6.3-Josh.6.4">v. 3, 4</reference>. This was all they were to do. 2. He assures them that on the seventh day before night they should, without fail, be masters of the town. Up on a signal given, they must all shout, and immediately the wall should fall down, which would not only expose the inhabitants, but so dispirit them that they would not be able to make any resistance, <reference osisRef="Josh.6.5">v. 5</reference>. God appointed this way, (1.) To magnify his own power, that he might be <hi type="italic">exalted in his own strength</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.21.13">Ps. xxi. 13</reference>), not in the strength of instruments. God would hereby yet further make bare his own almighty arm for the encouragement of Israel and the terror and confusion of the Canaanites. (2.) To put an honour upon his ark, the instituted token of his presence, and to give a reason for the laws by which the people were obliged to look upon it with the most profound veneration and respect. When, long after this, the ark was brought into the camp without orders from God, it was looked upon as a profanation of it, and the people paid dearly for their presumption, <reference osisRef="1Sam.4.3">1 Sam. iv. 3</reference>, &c. But now that it was done by the divine appointment it was an honour to the ark of God, and a great encouragement to the faith of Israel. (3.) It was likewise to put honour upon the priests, who were appointed upon this occasion to carry the ark and sound the trumpets. Ordinarily the priests were excused from war, but that this privilege, with other honours and powers that the law had given them, might not be grudged them, in this service they are principally employed, and so the people are made sensible what blessings they were to the public and how well worthy of all the advantages conferred upon them. (4.) It was to try the faith, obedience, and patience, of the people, to try whether they would observe a precept which to human policy seemed foolish to obey and believe a promise which in human probability seemed impossible to be performed. They were also proved whether they could patiently bear the reproaches of their enemies and patiently wait for the salvation of the Lord. Thus by faith, not by force, the walls of Jericho fell down. (5.) It was to encourage the hope of Israel with reference to the remaining difficulties that were before them. That suggestion of the evil spies that Canaan could never be conquered because the cities were <hi type="italic">walled up to heaven</hi> (<reference osisRef="Deut.1.28">Deut. i. 28</reference>) would by this be for ever silenced. The strongest and highest walls cannot hold out against Omnipotence; they needed not to fight, and therefore needed not to fear, because God fought for them.
entries.358bf6e57362f3d6c9f1e14819ee9ae9fbadbc04: <div eID="gen4206" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4207" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">6</hi> And Joshua the son of Nun called the priests, and said unto them, Take up the ark of the covenant, and let seven priests bear seven trumpets of rams' horns before the ark of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">7</hi> And he said unto the people, Pass on, and compass the city, and let him that is armed pass on before the ark of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">8</hi> And it came to pass, when Joshua had spoken unto the people, that the seven priests bearing the seven trumpets of rams' horns passed on before the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and blew with the trumpets: and the ark of the covenant of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> followed them. <hi type="super">9</hi> And the armed men went before the priests that blew with the trumpets, and the rereward came after the ark, <hi type="italic">the priests</hi> going on, and blowing with the trumpets. <hi type="super">10</hi> And Joshua had commanded the people, saying, Ye shall not shout, nor make any noise with your voice, neither shall <hi type="italic">any</hi> word proceed out of your mouth, until the day I bid you shout; then shall ye shout. <hi type="super">11</hi> So the ark of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> compassed the city, going about <hi type="italic">it</hi> once: and they came into the camp, and lodged in the camp. <hi type="super">12</hi> And Joshua rose early in the morning, and the priests took up the ark of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">13</hi> And seven priests bearing seven trumpets of rams' horns before the ark of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> went on continually, and blew with the trumpets: and the armed men went before them; but the rereward came after the ark of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , <hi type="italic">the priests</hi> going on, and blowing with the trumpets. <hi type="super">14</hi> And the second day they compassed the city once, and returned into the camp: so they did six days. <hi type="super">15</hi> And it came to pass on the seventh day, that they rose early about the dawning of the day, and compassed the city after the same manner seven times: only on that day they compassed the city seven times. <hi type="super">16</hi> And it came to pass at the seventh time, when the priests blew with the trumpets, Joshua said unto the people, Shout; for the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath given you the city. <div eID="gen4207" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4208" type="x-p"/> We have here an account of the cavalcade which Israel made about Jericho, the orders Joshua gave concerning it, as he had received them from the Lord and their punctual observance of these orders. We do not find that he gave the people the express assurances God had given him that he would deliver the city into their hands; but he tried whether they would obey orders with a general confidence that it would end well, and we find them very observant both of God and Joshua. <div eID="gen4208" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4209" type="x-p"/> I. Wherever the ark went the people attended it, <reference osisRef="Josh.6.9">v. 9</reference>. The armed men went before it to clear the way, not thinking it any disparagement to them, though they were men of war, to be pioneers to the ark of God. If any obstacle should be found in crossing the roads that led to the city (which they must do in walking round it) they would remove it; if any opposition should be made by the enemy, they would encounter it, that the priests' march with the ark might be easy and safe. It is an honour to the greatest men to do any good office to the ark and to serve the interests of religion in their country. The <hi type="italic">rereward,</hi> either another body of armed men, or Dan's squadron, which marched last through the wilderness, or, as some think, the multitude of the people who were not armed or disciplined for war (as many of them as would) followed the ark, to testify their respect to it, to grace the solemnity, and to be witnesses of what was done. Every faithful zealous Israelite would be willing to undergo the same fatigues and run the same hazard with the priests that bore the ark. <div eID="gen4209" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4210" type="x-p"/> II. Seven priests went immediately before the ark, having trumpets in their hands, with which they were continually sounding, <reference osisRef="Josh.6.4-Josh.6.5">v. 4, 5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Josh.6.9">9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Josh.6.13">13</reference>. The priests were God's ministers, and thus in his name, 1. They proclaimed war with the Canaanites, and so stuck a terror upon them; for by terrors upon their spirits they were to be conquered and subdued. Thus God's ministers, by the solemn declarations of his wrath against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of men, must blow the trumpet in Zion, and sound an alarm in the holy mountain, that the sinners in Zion may be afraid. They are God's heralds to denounce war against all those that go on still in their trespasses, but say, "We shall have peace, though we go on." 2. They proclaimed God's gracious presence with Israel, and so put life and courage into them. It was appointed that when they went to war the priests should encourage them with the assurance of God's presence with them, <reference osisRef="Deut.20.2-Deut.20.4">Deut. xx. 2-4</reference>. And particularly their blowing with trumpets was to be a sign to the people that they should be remembered before the Lord Their God in the day of battle, <reference osisRef="Num.10.9">Num. x. 9</reference>. It encouraged Abijah, <reference osisRef="2Chr.13.12">2 Chron. xiii. 12</reference>. Thus God's ministers, by sounding the Jubilee trumpet of the everlasting gospel, which proclaims liberty and victory, must encourage the good soldiers of Jesus Christ in their spiritual warfare. <div eID="gen4210" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4211" type="x-p"/> III. The trumpets they used were not those silver trumpets which were appointed to be made for their ordinary service, but trumpets of rams' horns, bored hollow for the purpose, as some think. These trumpets were of the basest matter, dullest sound, and least show, that the excellency of the power might be of God. Thus by the foolishness of preaching, fitly compared to the sounding of these rams' horns, the devil's kingdom is thrown down; and the <hi type="italic">weapons of our warfare,</hi> though they are not carnal nor seem to a carnal eye likely to bring any thing to pass, are yet <hi type="italic">mighty through God to the pulling down of strong-holds,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.10.4-2Cor.10.5">2 Cor. x. 4, 5</reference>. The word here is <hi type="italic">trumpets of Jobel,</hi> that is, such trumpets as they used to blow withal in the year of jubilee; so many interpreters understand it, as signifying the complete liberty to which Israel was now brought, and the bringing of the land of Canaan into the hands of its just and rightful owners. <div eID="gen4211" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4212" type="x-p"/> IV. All the people were commanded to be silent, not to speak a word, nor make any noise (<reference osisRef="Josh.6.10">v. 10</reference>), that they might the more carefully attend to the sound of the sacred trumpets, which they were now to look upon as the voice of God among them; and it does not become us to speak when God is speaking. It likewise intimates their reverent expectation of the event. <reference osisRef="Zech.2.13">Zech. ii. 13</reference>, <hi type="italic">Be silent, O all flesh, before the Lord.</hi> <reference osisRef="Exod.14.14">Exod. xiv. 14</reference>, <hi type="italic">God shall fight, and you shall hold your peace.</hi> <div eID="gen4212" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4213" type="x-p"/> V. They were to do this once a day for six days together and seven times the seventh day, and they did so, <reference osisRef="Josh.6.14-Josh.6.15">v. 14, 15</reference>. God could have caused the walls of Jericho to fall upon the first surrounding of them, but they must go round them thirteen times before they fall, that they might be kept waiting patiently for the Lord. Though they had lately come into Canaan, and their time was very precious (for they had a great deal of work before them), yet they must linger so many days about Jericho, seeming to do nothing, nor to make any progress in their business. As promised deliverances must be expected in God's way, so they must be expected in his time. <hi type="italic">He that believes does not make haste,</hi> not more haste than God would have him make. <hi type="italic">Go yet seven times,</hi> before any thing hopeful appears, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.43">1 Kings xviii. 43</reference>. <div eID="gen4213" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4214" type="x-p"/> VI. One of these days must needs be a sabbath day, and the Jews say that it was the last, but this is not certain; however, if he that appointed them to rest on the other sabbath days appointed them to walk on this, that was sufficient to justify them in it; he never intended to bind himself by his own laws, but that when he pleased he might dispense with them. The impotent man went upon this principle when he argued (<reference osisRef="John.5.11">John v. 11</reference>), <hi type="italic">He that made me whole</hi> (and therefore has a divine power) <hi type="italic">said unto me, Take up thy bed.</hi> And, in this case here, it was an honour to the sabbath day, by which our time is divided into weeks, that just seven days were to be spent in this work, and seven priests were employed to sound seven trumpets, this number being, on this occasion, as well as many others, made remarkable, in remembrance of the six day's work of creation and the seventh day's rest from it. And, besides, the law of the sabbath forbids our own work, which is servile and secular, but this which they did was a religious act. It is certainly no breach of the sabbath rest to do the sabbath work, for the sake of which the rest was instituted; and what is the sabbath work but to attend the ark in all its motions? <div eID="gen4214" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4215" type="x-p"/> VII. They continued to do this during the time appointed, and seven times the seventh day, though they saw not any effect of it, believing that <hi type="italic">at the end the vision would speak and not lie,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hab.2.3">Hab. ii. 3</reference>. If we persevere in the way of duty, we shall lose nothing by it in the long run. It is probable they walked at such a distance from the walls as to be out of the reach of the enemies' arrows and out of the hearing of their scoffs. We may suppose the oddness of the thing did at first amuse the besieged, but by the seventh day they had grown secure, feeling no harm from that which perhaps they looked upon as an enchantment. Probably they bantered the besiegers, as those mentioned in <reference osisRef="Neh.4.2">Neh. iv. 2</reference>, "<hi type="italic">What do these feeble Jews?</hi> Is this the people we thought so formidable? Are these their methods of attack?" Thus they cried peace and safety, that the destruction might be the more terrible when it came. <hi type="italic">Wicked men</hi> (says bishop Hall) <hi type="italic">think God in jest when he is preparing for their judgment;</hi> but they will be convinced of their mistake when it is too late. <div eID="gen4215" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4216" type="x-p"/> VIII. At last they were to give a shout, and did so, and immediately the walls fell, <reference osisRef="Josh.6.16">v. 16</reference>. This was a shout for mastery, a triumphant shout; the <hi type="italic">shout of a king is among them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Num.23.21">Num. xxiii. 21</reference>. This was a shout of faith; they believed that the walls of Jericho would fall, and by this faith the walls were thrown down. It was a shot of prayer, an echo to the sound of the trumpets which proclaimed the promise that God would remember them; with one accord, as one man, they cry to heaven for help, and help comes in. Some allude to this to show that we must never expect a complete victory over our own corruptions till the very evening of our last day, and then we shall shout in triumph over them, <hi type="italic">when we come to the number and measure of our perfection,</hi> as bishop Hall expresses it. <hi type="italic">A good heart</hi> (says he) <hi type="italic">groans under the sense of his infirmities, fain would be rid of them, and strives and prays, but, when all is done, until the end of the seventh day it cannot be;</hi> then judgment shall be brought forth unto victory. And at the end of time, when our Lord shall descend from heaven with a shout, and the sound of a trumpet, Satan's kingdom shall be completely ruined, and not till then, when all opposing rule, principality, and power, shall be effectually and eternally put down.
entries.dfc4cd7098cb5b3d89187578595e93b06e463f46: <div eID="gen4216" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Jericho Destroyed; Preservation of Rahab. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1451.)</title> <div sID="gen4217" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">17</hi> And the city shall be accursed, <hi type="italic">even</hi> it, and all that <hi type="italic">are</hi> therein, to the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : only Rahab the harlot shall live, she and all that <hi type="italic">are</hi> with her in the house, because she hid the messengers that we sent. <hi type="super">18</hi> And ye, in any wise keep <hi type="italic">yourselves</hi> from the accursed thing, lest ye make <hi type="italic">yourselves</hi> accursed, when ye take of the accursed thing, and make the camp of Israel a curse, and trouble it. <hi type="super">19</hi> But all the silver, and gold, and vessels of brass and iron, <hi type="italic">are</hi> consecrated unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : they shall come into the treasury of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">20</hi> So the people shouted when <hi type="italic">the priests</hi> blew with the trumpets: and it came to pass, when the people heard the sound of the trumpet, and the people shouted with a great shout, that the wall fell down flat, so that the people went up into the city, every man straight before him, and they took the city. <hi type="super">21</hi> And they utterly destroyed all that <hi type="italic">was</hi> in the city, both man and woman, young and old, and ox, and sheep, and ass, with the edge of the sword. <hi type="super">22</hi> But Joshua had said unto the two men that had spied out the country, Go into the harlot's house, and bring out thence the woman, and all that she hath, as ye sware unto her. <hi type="super">23</hi> And the young men that were spies went in, and brought out Rahab, and her father, and her mother, and her brethren, and all that she had; and they brought out all her kindred, and left them without the camp of Israel. <hi type="super">24</hi> And they burnt the city with fire, and all that <hi type="italic">was</hi> therein: only the silver, and the gold, and the vessels of brass and of iron, they put into the treasury of the house of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">25</hi> And Joshua saved Rahab the harlot alive, and her father's household, and all that she had; and she dwelleth in Israel <hi type="italic">even</hi> unto this day; because she hid the messengers, which Joshua sent to spy out Jericho. <hi type="super">26</hi> And Joshua adjured <hi type="italic">them</hi> at that time, saying, Cursed <hi type="italic">be</hi> the man before the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , that riseth up and buildeth this city Jericho: he shall lay the foundation thereof in his firstborn, and in his youngest <hi type="italic">son</hi> shall he set up the gates of it. <hi type="super">27</hi> So the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> was with Joshua; and his fame was <hi type="italic">noised</hi> throughout all the country. <div eID="gen4217" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4218" type="x-p"/> The people had religiously observed the orders given them concerning the besieging of Jericho, and now at length Joshua had told them (<reference osisRef="Josh.6.16">v. 16</reference>), "<hi type="italic">The Lord hath given you the city,</hi> enter and take possession." Accordingly in these verses we have, <div eID="gen4218" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4219" type="x-p"/> I. The rules they were to observe in taking possession. God gives it to them, and therefore may direct it to what uses and intents, and clog it with what provisos and limitations he thinks fit. It is given to them to be devoted to God, as the first and perhaps the worst of all the cities of Canaan. 1. The city must be burnt, and all the lives in it sacrificed without mercy to the justice of God. All this they knew was included in those words, <reference osisRef="Josh.6.17">v. 17</reference>. The city shall be a <hi type="italic">cherem,</hi> a devoted thing, at and all therein, to the Lord. No life in it might be ransomed upon any terms; they must all be surely <hi type="italic">put to death,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lev.27.29">Lev. xxvii. 29</reference>. So he appoints from whom as creatures they had received their lives, and to whom as sinners they had forfeited them; and who may dispute his sentence? <hi type="italic">Is God unrighteous, who</hi> thus <hi type="italic">taketh vengeance?</hi> God forbid we should entertain such a thought! There was more of God seen in the taking of Jericho than of any other of the cities of Canaan, and therefore that must be more than any other devoted to him. And the severe usage of this city would strike a terror upon all the rest and melt their hearts yet more before Israel. Only, when this severity is ordered, Rahab and her family are excepted: <hi type="italic">She shall live and all that are with her.</hi> She had distinguished herself from her neighbours by the kindness she showed to Israel, and therefore shall be distinguished from them by the speedy return of that kindness. 2. All the treasure of it, the money and plate and valuable goods, must be consecrated to the service of the tabernacle, and brought into the stock of dedicated things, the Jews say because the city was taken on the sabbath day. Thus God would be honoured by the beautifying and enriching of his tabernacle; thus preparation was made for the extraordinary expenses of his service; and thus the Israelites were taught not to set their hearts upon worldly wealth nor to aim at heaping up abundance of it for themselves. God had promised them a land <hi type="italic">flowing with milk and honey,</hi> not a land abounding with silver and gold; for he would have them live comfortably in it, that they might serve him cheerfully, but not covet either to trade with distant countries or to hoard for after times. He would likewise have them to reckon themselves enriched in the enriching of the tabernacle, and to think that which was laid up in God's house as truly their honour and wealth as if it had been laid up in their own. 3. A particular caution is given them to take heed of meddling with the forbidden spoil; for what was devoted to God, if they offered to appropriate it to their own use, would prove accursed to them; therefore (<reference osisRef="Josh.6.18">v. 18</reference>) "<hi type="italic">In any wise keep yourselves from the accursed thing;</hi> you will find yourselves inclined to reach towards it, but check yourselves, and frighten yourselves from having any thing to do with it." He speaks as if he foresaw the sin of Achan, which we have an account of in the next chapter, when he gives this reason for the caution, <hi type="italic">lest you make the camp of Israel a curse and trouble it,</hi> as it proved that Achan did. <div eID="gen4219" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4220" type="x-p"/> II. The entrance that was opened to them into the city by the sudden fall of the walls, or at least that part of the wall over against which they then were when they gave the shout (<reference osisRef="Josh.6.20">v. 20</reference>): <hi type="italic">The wall fell down flat,</hi> and probably killed abundance of people, the guards that stood sentinel upon it, or others that crowded about it, to look at the Israelites that were walking round. We read of thousands killed by the fall of a wall, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.20.30">1 Kings xx. 30</reference>. That which they trusted to for defence proved their destruction. The sudden fall of the wall, no doubt, put the inhabitants into such a consternation that they had no strength nor spirit to make any resistance, but they became an easy prey to the sword of Israel, and saw to how little purpose it was to shut their gates against a people that had <hi type="italic">the Lord on the head of them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mic.2.13">Mic. ii. 13</reference>. Note, The God of heaven easily can, and certainly will, break down all the opposing power of his and his church's enemies. Gates of brass and bars of iron are, before him, but as straw and rotten wood, <reference osisRef="Isa.45.1-Isa.45.2">Isa. xlv. 1, 2</reference>. <hi type="italic">Who will bring me into the strong city? Wilt not thou, O God?</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.60.9-Ps.60.10">Ps. lx. 9, 10</reference>. Thus shall Satan's kingdom fall, nor shall any prosper that harden themselves against God. <div eID="gen4220" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4221" type="x-p"/> III. The execution of the orders given concerning this devoted city. All that breathed were put to the sword; not only the men that were found in arms, but the women, and children, and old people. Though they cried for quarter, and begged ever so earnestly for their lives, there was no room for compassion, pity must be forgotten: they <hi type="italic">utterly destroyed all,</hi> <reference osisRef="Josh.6.21">v. 21</reference>. If they had not had a divine warrant under the seal of miracles for this execution, it could not have been justified, nor can it justify the like now, when we are sure no such warrant can be produced. But, being appointed by the righteous Judge of heaven and earth to do it, who is not unrighteous in taking vengeance, they are to be applauded in doing it as the faithful ministers of his justice. Work for God was then bloody work; and <hi type="italic">cursed was he that did it deceitfully, keeping back his sword from blood,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.48.10">Jer. xlviii. 10</reference>. But the spirit of the gospel is very different, for Christ came not to destroy men's lives but to save them, <reference osisRef="Luke.9.56">Luke ix. 56</reference>. Christ's victories were of another nature. The cattle were put to death with the owners, as additional sacrifices to the divine justice. The cattle of the Israelites, when slain at the altar, were accepted as sacrifices <hi type="italic">for</hi> them, but the cattle of these Canaanites were required to be slain as sacrifices <hi type="italic">with</hi> them, for their iniquity was not to be purged with sacrifice and offering: both were for the glory of God. 2. The city was <hi type="italic">burnt with fire, and all that was in it,</hi> <reference osisRef="Josh.6.24">v. 24</reference>. The Israelites, perhaps, when they had taken Jericho, a large and well-built city, hoped they should have that for their head-quarters; but God will have them yet to dwell in tents, and therefore fires this nest, lest they should nestle in it. 3. All the silver and gold, and all those vessels which were capable of being purified by fire, were brought into the treasury of the house of the Lord; not that he needed it but that he would be honoured by it, as the Lord of hosts, of their hosts in particular, the God that gave the victory and therefore might demand the spoil, either the whole, as here, or, as sometimes, a tenth, <reference osisRef="Heb.7.4">Heb. vii. 4</reference>. <div eID="gen4221" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4222" type="x-p"/> IV. The preservation of Rahab the harlot, or inn-keeper, who <hi type="italic">perished not with those that believed not,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.11.31">Heb. xi. 31</reference>. The public faith was engaged for her safety by the two spies, who acted therein as public persons; and therefore, though the hurry they were in at the taking of the town was no doubt very great, yet Joshua took effectual care for her preservation. The same persons that she had secured were employed to secure her, <reference osisRef="Josh.6.22-Josh.6.23">v. 22, 23</reference>. They were best able to do it who knew her and her house, and they were fittest to do it, that it might appear it was for the sake of her kindness to them that she was thus distinguished and had her life given her for a prey. All her kindred were saved with her; like Noah she <hi type="italic">believed to the saving of her house;</hi> and thus faith in Christ <hi type="italic">brings salvation to the house,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.16.31">Acts xvi. 31</reference>. Some ask how her house, which is said to have been <hi type="italic">upon the wall</hi> (<reference osisRef="Josh.2.15">ch. ii. 15</reference>), escaped falling with the wall; we are sure it did escape, for she and her relations were safe in it, either though it joined so near to the wall as to be said to be <hi type="italic">upon it,</hi> yet it was so far off as not to fall either with the wall or under it; or, rather, that part of the wall on which her house stood fell not. Now being preserved alive, 1. She was left for some time without the camp to be purified from the Gentile superstition, which she was to renounce, and to be prepared for her admission as a proselyte. 2. She was in due time incorporated with the church of Israel, and she and her posterity dwelt in Israel, and her family was remarkable long after. We find her the wife of Salmon, prince of Judah, mother of Boaz, and named among the ancestors of our Saviour, <reference osisRef="Matt.1.5">Matt. i. 5</reference>. Having received Israelites in the name of Israelites, she had an Israelite's reward. Bishop Pierson observes that Joshua's saving Rahab the harlot, and admitting her into Israel, were a figure of Christ's receiving into his kingdom, and entertaining there, the publicans and the harlots, <reference osisRef="Matt.21.31">Matt. xxi. 31</reference>. Or it may be applied to the conversion of the Gentiles. <div eID="gen4222" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4223" type="x-p"/> V. Jericho is condemned to a perpetual desolation, and a curse pronounced upon the man that at any time hereafter should offer to rebuild it (<reference osisRef="Josh.6.26">v. 26</reference>): <hi type="italic">Joshua adjured them,</hi> that is, the elders and people of Israel, not only by their own consent, obliging themselves and their posterity never to rebuild this city, but by the divine appointment, God himself having forbidden it under the severe penalty here annexed. 1. God would hereby show the weight of a divine curse; where it rests there is no contending with it nor getting from under it; it brings ruin without remedy or repair. 2. He would have it to remain in its ruins a standing monument of his wrath against the Canaanites when the measure of their iniquity was full, and of his mercy to his people when the time had come for their settlement in Canaan. The desolations of their enemies were witnesses of his favour to them, and would upbraid them with their ingratitude to that God who had done so much for them. The situation of the city was very pleasant, and probably its nearness to Jordan was an advantage to it, which would tempt men to build upon the same spot; but they are here told it is at their peril if they do it. Men build for their posterity, but he that builds Jericho shall have no posterity to enjoy what he builds; his eldest son shall die when he begins the work, and if he take not warning by that stroke to desist, but will go on presumptuously, the finishing of his work shall be attended with the funeral of his youngest, and we must suppose all the rest cut off between. This curse, not being a <hi type="italic">curse causeless,</hi> did come upon that man who long after rebuilded Jericho (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.16.34">1 Kings xvi. 34</reference>), but we are not to think it made the place ever the worse when it was built, or brought any hurt to those that inhabited it. We find Jericho afterwards graced with the presence, not only of those two great prophets Elijah and Elisha, but of our blessed Saviour himself, <reference osisRef="Luke.18.35">Luke xviii. 35</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.19.1">xix. 1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.20.29">Matt. xx. 29</reference>. Note, It is a dangerous thing to attempt the building up of that which God will have to be destroyed. See <reference osisRef="Mal.1.4">Mal. i. 4</reference>. <div eID="gen4223" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4224" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Lastly,</hi> All this magnified Joshua and raised his reputation (<reference osisRef="Josh.6.27">v. 27</reference>); it made him not only acceptable to Israel, but formidable to the Canaanites, because it appeared that God was with him of a truth: the Word of the Lord was with him, so the Chaldee, even Christ himself, the same that was with Moses. Nothing can more raise a man's reputation, nor make him appear more truly great, than to have the evidences of God's presence with him.  <chapter eID="Josh.6"/> <div eID="gen4224" type="x-p"/>

entries.99382b7c10c1a1f1834687379c2910ce2a1e000b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2016"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 6</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Josh.6.1-Josh.6.7">Jos 6:1-7</reference>. Jericho Shut Up.</title> <div sID="gen2688" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2016"/><hi type="bold">1. Now Jericho was straitly shut up--</hi>This verse is a parenthesis introduced to prepare the way for the directions given by the Captain of the Lord's host. <div eID="gen2688" type="x-p"/>
entries.2387b8bbb50d55d814bfa9fe566462130feb34eb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2017"/><div sID="gen2689" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2017"/><hi type="bold">2. See, I have given into thine hand Jericho--</hi>The language intimates that a purpose already formed was about to be carried into immediate execution; and that, although the king and inhabitants of Jericho were fierce and experienced warriors, who would make a stout and determined resistance, the Lord promised a certain and easy victory over them. <div eID="gen2689" type="x-p"/>
entries.d929684e84826eae5dc9861bd16c6e00c6bcdd2b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2018"/><div sID="gen2690" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2018"/><hi type="bold">3-5. ye shall compass the city, all ye men of war. ... Thus shalt thou do six days, &c.--</hi>Directions are here given as to the mode of procedure. Hebrew, "horns of jubilee"; that is, the bent or crooked trumpets with which the jubilee was proclaimed. It is probable that the horns of this animal were used at first; and that afterwards, when metallic trumpets were introduced, the primitive name, as well as form of them, was traditionally continued. The design of this whole proceeding was obviously to impress the Canaanites with a sense of the divine omnipotence, to teach the Israelites a memorable lesson of faith and confidence in God's promises, and to inspire sentiments of respect and reverence for the ark as the symbol of His presence. The length of time during which those circuits were made tended the more intensely to arrest the attention, and to deepen the impressions, both of the Israelites and the enemy. The number seven was among the Israelites the symbolic seal of the covenant between God and their nation [Keil, Hengstenberg]. <div eID="gen2690" type="x-p"/>
entries.dcb749fee17af19046fa541e405b88cbce06ec31: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2019"/><div sID="gen2691" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2019"/><hi type="bold">6-7. Joshua ... called the priests--</hi>The pious leader, whatever military preparations he had made, surrendered all his own views, at once and unreservedly, to the declared will of God. <div eID="gen2691" type="x-p"/>
entries.f241a1d979e2ea991f2a2b89232df4c08963837a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2020"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Josh.6.8-Josh.6.19">Jos 6:8-19</reference>. The City Compassed Six Days.</title> <div sID="gen2692" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2020"/><hi type="bold">8-11. the seven priests bearing the seven trumpets ... passed on before the Lord--</hi>before the ark, called "the ark of the covenant," for it contained the tables on which the covenant was inscribed. The procession was made in deep and solemn silence, conforming to the instructions given to the people by their leader at the outset, that they were to refrain from all acclamation and noise of any kind until he should give them a signal. It must have been a strange sight; no mound was raised, no sword drawn, no engine planted, no pioneers undermining--here were armed men, but no stroke given; they must walk and not fight. Doubtless the people of Jericho made themselves merry with the spectacle [Bishop Hall]. <div eID="gen2692" type="x-p"/>
entries.19a7d3d6dbb119571c295e40f7e2f43f7ea8ea37: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2021"/><div sID="gen2693" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2021"/><hi type="bold">12-14. Joshua rose early in the morning, and the priests took up the ark of the Lord--</hi>The second day's procession seems to have taken place in the morning. In all other respects, down even to the smallest details, the arrangements of the first day continued to be the rule followed on the other six. <div eID="gen2693" type="x-p"/>
entries.315cdb17d06276c7657c8faa958bbe9589e00d57: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2022"/><div sID="gen2694" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2022"/><hi type="bold">15. on the seventh day, that they rose early about the dawning of the day, and compassed the city ... seven times--</hi>on account of the seven circuits they had to make that day. It is evident, however, that the militia only of the Israelites had been called to the march--for it is inconceivable that two millions of people could have gone so frequently round the city in a day. <div eID="gen2694" type="x-p"/>
entries.4d2be7e4ff6ab0980467a2f9d3b55579027ea22a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2023"/><div sID="gen2695" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2023"/><hi type="bold">16. it came to pass at the seventh time, ... Joshua said unto the people, Shout; for the Lord hath given you the city--</hi>This delay brought out their faith and obedience in so remarkable a manner, that it is celebrated by the apostle (<reference osisRef="Heb.11.30">He 11:30</reference>). <div eID="gen2695" type="x-p"/>
entries.79799f1ab43358260f90a26bf891b4684b5b0b23: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2024"/><div sID="gen2696" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2024"/><hi type="bold">17-19. And the city shall be accursed--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Lev.27.28">Le 27:28</reference>). The cherem, or "anathema," was a devotion to utter destruction (<reference osisRef="Deut.7.2">De 7:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.20.17">20:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.3">1Sa 15:3</reference>). When such a ban was pronounced against a hostile city, the men and animals were killed--no booty was allowed to be taken. The idols and all the precious ornaments on them were to be burned (<reference osisRef="Deut.7.25">De 7:25</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="1Chr.14.12">1Ch 14:12</reference>). Everything was either to be destroyed or consecrated to the sanctuary. Joshua pronounced this ban on Jericho, a great and wealthy city, evidently by divine direction. The severity of the doom, accordant with the requirements of a law which was holy, just, and good, was justified, not only by the fact of its inhabitants being part of a race who had filled up their iniquities, but by their resisting the light of the recent astonishing miracle at the Jordan. Besides, as Jericho seems to have been defended by reinforcements from all the country (<reference osisRef="Josh.24.11">Jos 24:11</reference>), its destruction would paralyze all the rest of the devoted people, and thus tend to facilitate the conquest of the land; showing, as so astounding a military miracle did, that it was done, not by man, but by the power and through the anger, of God. <div eID="gen2696" type="x-p"/>
entries.9ca8756bc6f096ca3391e853aa853f34f45c302d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2026"/><div sID="gen2699" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2026"/><hi type="bold">20-21. So the people shouted when the priests blew with the trumpets--</hi>Towards the close of the seventh circuit, the signal was given by Joshua, and on the Israelites' raising their loud war cry, the walls fell down, doubtless burying multitudes of the inhabitants in the ruins, while the besiegers, rushing in, consigned everything animate and inanimate to indiscriminate destruction (<reference osisRef="Deut.20.16">De 20:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.20.17">17</reference>). Jewish writers mention it as an immemorial tradition that the city fell on the Sabbath. It should be remembered that the Canaanites were incorrigible idolaters, addicted to the most horrible vices, and that the righteous judgment of God might sweep them away by the sword, as well as by famine or pestilence. There was mercy mingled with judgment in employing the sword as the instrument of punishing the guilty Canaanites, for while it was directed against one place, time was afforded for others to repent. <div eID="gen2699" type="x-p"/>
entries.ae7c785cc70ebdf8e6d348faf70cbdf8025dbd5b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2027"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Josh.6.22-Josh.6.25">Jos 6:22-25</reference>. Rahab Is Saved.</title> <div sID="gen2700" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2027"/><hi type="bold">22-23. Joshua had said ... Go into the harlot's house, and bring out thence the woman, and all that she hath--</hi>It is evident that the town walls were not demolished universally, at least all at once, for Rahab's house was allowed to stand until her relatives were rescued according to promise. <div eID="gen2700" type="x-p"/>
entries.137b1587163d6ef360dfaf0d35098281cdceab31: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2029"/><div sID="gen2702" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2029"/><hi type="bold">24. burned the city ... and all ... therein--</hi>except the silver, gold, and other metals, which, as they would not burn, were added to the treasury of the sanctuary. <div eID="gen2702" type="x-p"/>
entries.a5a6f364b60b82d81ef3773fda331008697fbb69: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2030"/><div sID="gen2703" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2030"/><hi type="bold">25. she--</hi>Rahab<div eID="gen2703" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2704" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">dwelleth in Israel unto this day--</hi>a proof that this book was written not long after the events related.<div eID="gen2704" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2705" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Josh.6.26">Jos 6:26</reference>, <reference osisRef="Josh.6.27">27</reference>. The Rebuilder of Jericho Cursed. <div eID="gen2705" type="x-p"/>
entries.f7cfa7159f50b85ce4c5b42d65e81ef7f2b1d5e8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2031"/><div sID="gen2706" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2031"/><hi type="bold">26. Joshua adjured them at that time--</hi>that is, imposed upon his countrymen a solemn oath, binding on themselves as well as their posterity, that they would never rebuild that city. Its destruction was designed by God to be a permanent memorial of His abhorrence of idolatry and its attendant vices.<div eID="gen2706" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2707" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Cursed be the man ... that riseth up and buildeth this city Jericho--</hi>that is, makes the daring attempt to build.<div eID="gen2707" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2708" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he shall lay the foundation thereof in his first-born, and in his youngest son shall he set up the gates of it--</hi>shall become childless--the first beginning being marked by the death of his oldest son, and his only surviving child dying at the time of its completion. This curse was accomplished five hundred fifty years after its denunciation (see on <reference osisRef="1Kgs.16.34">1Ki 16:34</reference>). <chapter eID="Josh.6"/>

entries.0642622373a424efae86e691ee04d2f7dd8a5ece: <div eID="gen7538" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen7539" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen7540" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen7540" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen7539" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen7541" type="x-p"/> The inhabitants of Jericho close their gates, <reference osisRef="Jos.6.1">Jos 6:1</reference>. Continuation of the discourse between the captain of the Lord's host and Joshua. He commands the people to march round the city six days, the seven priests blowing with their trumpets; and to give a general shout, while marching round it on the seventh, and promises that then the walls of the city shall fall down, <reference osisRef="Jos.6.2-Jos.6.5">Jos 6:2-5</reference>. Joshua delivers these directions to the priests and to the people, <reference osisRef="Jos.6.6">Jos 6:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jos.6.7">Jos 6:7</reference>. The priests and people obey; the order of their procession, <reference osisRef="Jos.6.8-Jos.6.16">Jos 6:8-16</reference>. He commands them to spare the house of Rahab, <reference osisRef="Jos.6.17">Jos 6:17</reference>, and not to touch any part of the property of the city, the whole of which God had devoted to destruction, <reference osisRef="Jos.6.18">Jos 6:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jos.6.19">Jos 6:19</reference>. On the seventh day the walls fall down, and the Israelites take the city, <reference osisRef="Jos.6.20">Jos 6:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jos.6.21">Jos 6:21</reference>. The spies are ordered to take care of Rahab and her family - the city is burnt, but the silver, gold, brass, and iron, are put into the treasury of the house of the Lord, <reference osisRef="Jos.6.22-Jos.6.24">Jos 6:22-24</reference>. Rahab dwells among the Israelites, <reference osisRef="Jos.6.25">Jos 6:25</reference>; and the city is laid under a curse, <reference osisRef="Jos.6.26">Jos 6:26</reference>. <div eID="gen7541" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7542" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen7542" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7543" type="x-p"/> Now Jericho was straitly shut up - The king of Jericho, finding that the spies had escaped, though the city was always kept shut by night, took the most proper precaution to prevent every thing of the kind in future, by keeping the city shut both day and night, having, no doubt, laid in a sufficiency of provisions to stand a siege, being determined to defend himself to the uttermost.
entries.d17d58aec127f7dc19b1b466e58a28f9e0083468: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen7543" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7544" type="x-p"/> And the Lord said unto Joshua - This is the same person who in the preceding chapter is called the captain or prince of the Lord's host, the discourse being here continued that was begun at the conclusion of the preceding chapter, from which the first verses of this are unnaturally divided. <div eID="gen7544" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7545" type="x-p"/> I have given into thine hand Jericho, etc. - From <reference osisRef="Jos.24.11">Jos 24:11</reference>, it seems as if there had been persons of all the seven Canaanitish nations then in Jericho, who might have come together at this time to help the king of Jericho against the invading Israelites. The Targum intimates that the place was very strong, having "gates of iron and bars of brass; and was shut up so closely that none came out, either to combat or make offers of peace."
entries.56edc9e650fc61c9fee4ef4f997157225716fdad: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen7545" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7546" type="x-p"/> Ye shall compass the city - In what order the people marched round the city does not exactly appear from the text. Some think they observed the same order as in their ordinary marches in the desert; (see the note on <reference osisRef="Num.10.14">Num 10:14</reference>, and see the plans, <reference osisRef="Num.2.2">Num 2:2</reference> (note)); others think that the soldiers marched first, then the priests who blew the trumpets, then those who carried the ark, and lastly the people.
entries.329a1096c082d4fe3e77b0081f7fac42aeb956ae: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen7546" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7547" type="x-p"/> Seven trumpets of rams' horns - The Hebrew word יובלים yobelim does not signify rams' horns; (see the note on <reference osisRef="Lev.25.11">Lev 25:11</reference>); nor do any of the ancient versions, the Chaldee excepted, give it this meaning. The instruments used on this occasion were evidently of the same kind with those used on the jubilee, and were probably made of horn or of silver; and the text in this place may be translated, And seven priests shall bear before the ark the seven jubilee trumpets, for they appear to have been the same kind as those used on the jubilee. <div eID="gen7547" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7548" type="x-p"/> Seven times - The time was thus lengthened out that the besiegers and the besieged might be the more deeply impressed with that supernatural power by which alone the walls fell.
entries.0197cd81df2803c920d6388624282c46f11ca085: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen7548" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7549" type="x-p"/> The wall of the city shall fall down flat - Several commentators, both Jews and Christians, have supposed that the ground under the foundation of the walls opened, and the wall sunk into the chasm, so that there remained nothing but plain ground for the Israelites to walk over. Of this the text says nothing: - ונפלה חומת העיר תחתיה venaphelah chomath hair tachteyha, literally translated, is, The wall of the city shall fall down Under Itself; which appears to mean no more than, The wall shall fall down From Its Very Foundations. And this probably was the case in every part, though large breaches in different places might be amply sufficient to admit the armed men first, after whom the whole host might enter, in order to destroy the city.
entries.2eaf6315625028a96ee7cea6cfa741b753ff7930: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen7549" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7550" type="x-p"/> The rereward came after the ark - The word מאסף measseph, from אסף asaph, to collect or gather up, may signify either the rereward, as our translation understands it, or the people who carried the baggage of the army; for on the seventh day this was necessary, as much fighting might be naturally expected in the assault, and they would need a supply of arms, darts, etc., as well as conveniences for those who might happen to be wounded: or the persons here intended might be such as carried the sacred articles belonging to the ark, or merely such people as might follow in the procession, without observing any particular order. The Jews think the division of Dan is meant, which always brought up the rear. See <reference osisRef="Num.10.25">Num 10:25</reference>.
entries.3edeb2997ae66dfdca246e675b5d480ee69c86e1: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen7550" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7551" type="x-p"/> So they did six days - It is not likely that the whole Israelitish host went each day round the city. This would have been utterly impossible: the fighting men alone amounted to nearly 600,000, independently of the people, who must have amounted at least to two or three millions; we may therefore safely assert that only a select number, such as was deemed necessary for the occasion, were employed. Jericho could not have been a large city: and to reduce it could not have required a hundredth part of the armed force under the command of Joshua.
entries.b2eb3be35f51410c9f2205f585b4b8ffb5dd4e30: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen7551" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7552" type="x-p"/> The seventh day - they rose early - Because on this day they had to encompass the city seven times; a proof that the city could not have been very extensive, else this going round it seven times, and having time sufficient left to sack and destroy it, would have been impossible. It is evident that in the course of these seven days there must have been a Sabbath, and that on this Sabbath the host must have encompassed the city as on the other days: the Jews themselves allow this, and Rab. De Kimchi says "He who had ordained the observance of the Sabbath commanded it to be broken for the destruction of Jericho." But it does not appear that there could be any breach in the Sabbath by the people simply going round the city, the ark in company, and the priests sounding the sacred trumpets. This was a mere religious procession, performed at the command of God, in which no servile work was done. Therefore Marcion's objection, that the God of the Hebrews showed a changeableness of disposition in commanding the Sabbath to be kept sacred at one time, and then to be broken at another, is without foundation; for I must contend that no breach took place on this occasion, unless it could be made to appear that the day on which Jericho was taken was the Sabbath which is very unlikely, and which none can prove. But if even this were to be conceded, it is a sufficient answer to all such cavils, that the God who commanded the Sabbath to be set apart for rest and religious purposes, has always authority to suspend for a season the operation of merely ceremonial laws, or to abrogate them entirely, when the purpose of their institution is fulfilled. The Son of man is Lord even of the Sabbath.
entries.1ac259bc4f76a22daa679851f1e7c18d6adec100: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen7552" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7553" type="x-p"/> The city shall be accursed - That is, it shall be devoted to destruction; ye shall take no spoils, and put all that resist to the sword. Though this may be the meaning of the word חרם cherem in some places, see the note on <reference osisRef="Lev.27.29">Lev 27:29</reference>, yet here it seems to imply the total destruction of all the inhabitants, see <reference osisRef="Jos.6.21">Jos 6:21</reference>; but it is likely that peace was offered to this city, and that the extermination of the inhabitants was in consequence of the rejection of this offer.
entries.e7619112f8e7aef041b1b91e5b42cb53504d97ab: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen7553" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7554" type="x-p"/> But all the silver, and gold - shall come into the treasury - The Brahmins will receive from any caste, however degraded, gold, silver, etc.: but to receive from Shoodras food, garments, etc., would be considered a great degradation. - Ward.
entries.298713c489cf129128650d64412fd1875c738ab9: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen7554" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7555" type="x-p"/> The people shouted with a great shout, that the wall fell down - There has been much learned labor spent to prove that the shouting of the people might be the natural cause that the wall fell down! To wait here, either to detail or refute any such arguments, would be lost time: enough of them may be seen in Scheuchzer. The whole relation evidently supposes it to have been a supernatural interference, as the blowing of the trumpets, and the shouting of the people, were too contemptible to be used even as instruments in this work, with the expectation of accomplishing it in a natural way.
entries.9151ab02afe35316ad2385e2b193893617e39ef4: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen7555" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7556" type="x-p"/> They utterly destroyed - both man, and woman, etc. - As this act was ordered by God himself, who is the Maker and Judge of all men, it must be right: for the Judge of all the earth cannot do wrong. Nothing that breathed was permitted to live; hence the oxen, sheep, and asses, were destroyed, as well as the inhabitants.
entries.2a3e0f37ce889e806545bed08d9d4b16fa2fc4db: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen7556" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7557" type="x-p"/> Brought out Rahab, and her father, etc. - Rahab having been faithful to her vow of secrecy, the Israelites were bound by the oath of the spies, who acted as their representatives in this business, to preserve her and her family alive. <div eID="gen7557" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7558" type="x-p"/> And left them without the camp - They were considered as persons unclean, and consequently left without the camp; (see <reference osisRef="Lev.13.46">Lev 13:46</reference>; <reference osisRef="Num.12.14">Num 12:14</reference>). When they had abjured heathenism, were purified, and the males had received circumcision, they were doubtless admitted into the camp, and became incorporated with Israel.
entries.6dde04acf0218083dd84b5d7c8c9e70af026c182: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen7558" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7559" type="x-p"/> Only the silver, and the gold - they put into the treasury, etc. - The people were to have no share of the spoils, because they had no hand in the conquest. God alone overthrew the city; and into his treasury only the spoils were brought. This is one proof that the agitation of the air, by the sound of the people's voice, was not the cause of the fall of the city walls. <div eID="gen7559" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7560" type="x-p"/> Vessels of brass and of iron - Instead of כלי keley, Vessels, the Septuagint, in the Alexandrian copy, evidently have read כל col, All, with the omission of the י yod; for in <reference osisRef="Jos.6.19">Jos 6:19</reference> they translate πας χαλκος και σιδηρος, All the brass and iron: but this reading does not appear in any of Kennicott's or De Rossi's MSS.
entries.33877e28c33884b07709accc975dd9819b8a0cf4: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen7560" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7561" type="x-p"/> And she dwelleth in Israel even unto this day - This is one proof that the book was written in the time to which it is commonly referred; and certainly might have been done by the hand of Joshua himself, though doubtless many marginal notes may have since crept into the text, which, to superficial observers, give it the appearance of having been written after the days of Joshua. See the preface to this book.
entries.985a0d79d0e2bc192abeaf37301d13bb421335c8: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen7561" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7562" type="x-p"/> And Joshua adjured them at that time - It appears that he had received intimations from God that this idolatrous city should continue a monument of the Divine displeasure: and having convened the princes and elders of the people, he bound them by an oath that they should never rebuild it; and then, in their presence, pronounced a curse upon the person who should attempt it. The ruins of this city continuing would be a permanent proof, not only of God's displeasure against idolatry, but of the miracle which he had wrought in behalf of the Israelites; and for these reasons God willed that it should not be rebuilt: nevertheless, he left men to the operation of their own free will, and recorded the penalty which those must pay who should disobey him. <div eID="gen7562" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7563" type="x-p"/> He shall lay the foundation thereof, etc. - This is a strange execration; but it may rather be considered in the light of a prediction. It seems to intimate that he who should attempt to rebuild this city, should lose all his children in the interim, from laying the foundation to the completion of the walls; which the author of <reference osisRef="1Kgs.16.34">1Kgs 16:34</reference> says was accomplished in Hiel the Beth-elite, who rebuilt Jericho under the reign of Ahab, and laid the foundation of it in Abiram, his first-born, and set up its gates in his youngest son Segub: this was 550 years after Joshua pronounced the curse. But we are not sure that this means that the children either died a natural or violent death on this occasion for we may understand the history as relating to the slow progress of the work. Hiel having begun the work at the birth of his first-born, was not able to conclude before the birth of his last child, who was born many years after: and as their names are mentioned, it is very likely that the distance of time between the birth of each was well known when this history was written; and that the extraordinary length of time spent in the work, in which a multitude of vexatious delays had taken place, is that to which the prophetic execration relates. Yet the first opinion is the most probable. We must not suppose that Jericho had been wholly neglected from its overthrow by Joshua to the days of Hiel; if it be the same with the city of palm trees, mentioned <reference osisRef="Deu.34.3">Deu 34:3</reference>. We find it mentioned as an inhabited place in the beginning of <reference osisRef="Jdg.1.16">Jdg 1:16</reference>, a short time after the death of Joshua: And the children of the Kenite, Moses' father-in-law, went up out of the city of palm trees, with the children of Judah, etc.; and this said city (if the same with the city of palm trees) was taken from the Israelites by Eglon king of Moab, <reference osisRef="Jdg.3.13">Jdg 3:13</reference>. The ambassadors of David, who were disgracefully treated by Hanun king of the Ammonites, were commanded to tarry at Jericho till their beards should grow, <reference osisRef="2Sam.10.4">2Sam 10:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Sam.10.5">2Sam 10:5</reference>. It appears, therefore, that there was a city which went under this name long before the time of Hiel, unless we can suppose that the city of palm trees was a different place from Jericho, or that the name Jericho was given to some part of the circumjacent country after the city was destroyed, which is very probable. After Hiel had rebuilt this city, it became of considerable consequence in the land of Judea: the courses of priests lodged there, who served in their turns at the temple; see <reference osisRef="Luk.10.30">Luk 10:30</reference>. There was a school of the prophets there, which was visited by Elijah and Elisha, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.2.4">2Kgs 2:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.2.5">2Kgs 2:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.2.18">2Kgs 2:18</reference>; and it was at this city that our Lord miraculously healed blind Bartimeus, <reference osisRef="Mar.10.46">Mar 10:46</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luk.18.35">Luk 18:35</reference>, etc. At present, Jericho is almost entirely deserted, having but thirty or forty miserable cabins in it, which serve for a place of refuge to some wretched Moors and Arabs, who live there like beasts. The plain of Jericho, formerly so celebrated for its fertility, is at present uncultivated, producing nothing but a few wild trees, and some very indifferent fruits. See Calmet.
entries.803226878396086b1dc61f3d5aa83e62f218f2c4: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen7563" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7564" type="x-p"/> So the Lord was with Joshua - Giving him miraculous assistance in all his enterprises; and this was what he was naturally led to expect from the communication made to him by the captain of the Lord's host, <reference osisRef="Jos.5.14">Jos 5:14</reference>, etc. <div eID="gen7564" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7565" type="x-p"/> 1. Many attempts have been made either to deny the miracle in the fall of Jericho, or to account for it on natural causes. Reference has already been made to some of these in the note on <reference osisRef="Jos.6.20">Jos 6:20</reference>. But to those who believe the Divine authenticity of the New Testament, every objection of this kind is removed by the authority of the author of the Epistle to the Hebrews, <reference osisRef="Heb.11.30">Heb 11:30</reference>; By Faith the walls of Jericho fell down, after they had been compassed about seven days. Hence we find that it was a miraculous interference; and that Joshua's faith in the promise made to him by the captain of the Lord's host, was the instrument which God chose to employ in the accomplishment of this important purpose. <div eID="gen7565" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7566" type="x-p"/> 2. The same is said of Rahab: By Faith the harlot Rahab perished not with them that believed not, when she had received the spies with peace, <reference osisRef="Heb.11.31">Heb 11:31</reference>. She believed that the true God was on the side of the Hebrews, and that all opposition to them must be in vain; and this faith led her to put herself under the Divine protection, and in virtue of it she escaped the destruction that fell on her countrymen. Thus God has ever chosen to put honor on faith, as the instrument by which he will perform his greatest miracles of justice and mercy. God, who cannot lie, has given the promise; he that believes shall have it accomplished; for with God nothing shall be impossible, and all things are possible to him that believes. These are Scriptural maxims, and God cannot deny himself. <div eID="gen7566" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7567" type="x-p"/> 3. On the curse pronounced by Joshua on those who should rebuild Jericho, it may be necessary to make a few remarks. In ancient history we have many instances of execrations against those who should rebuild those cities which had been destroyed in war, the revival of whose power and influence was dreaded; especially such cities as had been remarkable for oppression, insolence, or perfidy. Strabo observes, lib. xiii., p. 898, ed. 1707, that Agamemnon pronounced execrations on those who should rebuild Troy, as Croesus did against those who should rebuild Sidena, in which the tyrant Glaucias had taken refuge; and this mode of execrating cities, according to Strabo, was an ancient custom - Ειτε και καταρασαμενου του Αγαμεμνονος κατα παλαιον εθος· καθαπερ και ὁ Κροισος εξελων την Σιδηνην, εις ἡν ὁ τυραννος κατεφυγε Γλαυκιας, αρας εθετο κατα των τειχιουντων παλιν τον τοπον. The Romans made a decree full of execrations against those who should rebuild Carthage, which had been the rival of their empire; and which, from its advantageous situation, might again become formidable should it be rebuilt. See Zonaras, Anal. The Ionians, according to Isocrates, pronounced the most awful execrations on those who should rebuild the temples destroyed by the Persians, that they might remain to posterity an endless monument of the impiety of those barbarians; and that none might put confidence in a people who were so wicked as to make war on the gods themselves. The other Greeks who had suffered by the Persians acted in the same way, leaving the desolated temples as a public monument of the enmity that should ever subsist between the two nations. See Calmet, and see the notes on <reference osisRef="Num.22.6">Num 22:6</reference>.  <chapter eID="Josh.6"/> <div eID="gen7567" type="x-p"/>

entries.7de586c34cf4d162ea57034f1fe9aca58f94776d: <reference osisRef="Josh.6.1">Jos 6:1</reference> <hi type="italic">“Jericho was shutting its gates</hi> (vid., Jdg 9:51), <hi type="italic">and closely shut.”</hi> The participles express the permanence of the situation, and the combination of the active and passive in the emphatic form מסגּרת (lxx συγκεκλεισμένη καὶ ὠχυρωμένη; <hi type="italic">Vulg</hi>. <hi type="italic">clausa erat atque munita</hi>) serves to strengthen the idea, to which still further emphasis is given by the clause, <hi type="italic">“no one was going out and in,”</hi> i.e., so firmly shut that no one could get out or in.
entries.e436318bae032a4bd700a9204c40ba263d65ad81: <reference osisRef="Josh.6.2-Josh.6.5">Jos 6:2-5</reference> <hi type="italic">“And the Lord said to Joshua:”</hi> this is the sequel to <reference osisRef="Josh.5.15">Jos 5:15</reference>, as <reference osisRef="Josh.6.1">Jos 6:1</reference> is merely a parenthesis and Jehovah is the prince of the army of Jehovah (<reference osisRef="Josh.5.14">Jos 5:14</reference>), or the angel of Jehovah, who is frequently identified with Jehovah (see Pentateuch, pp. 106ff.). <hi type="italic">“See, I</hi> <hi type="italic">have given into thy hand Jericho and its king, and the mighty men of valour.”</hi> (“Have given,” referring to the purpose of God, which was already resolved upon, though the fulfilment was still in the future.) <hi type="italic">“The mighty men of valour”</hi> (brave warriors) is in apposition to Jericho, regarded as a community, and its king. In <reference osisRef="Josh.6.3-Josh.6.5">Jos 6:3-5</reference> there follows an explanation of the way in which the Lord would give Jericho into the hand of Joshua. All the Israelitish men of war were to go round the town once a day for six days. אחת פּעם ... הקּיף, <hi type="italic">“going round about the city once,”</hi> serves as a fuller explanation of סבּותם <hi type="italic">(“ye shall compass”).</hi> As they marched in this manner round the city, seven priests were to carry seven jubilee trumpets before the ark, which implies that the ark itself was to be carried round the city in solemn procession. But on the seventh day they were to march round the town seven times, and the priests to blow the trumpets; and when there was a blast with the jubilee horn, and the people on hearing the sound of the trumpet raised a great cry, the wall of the town should fall down <hi type="italic">“under</hi> <hi type="italic">itself.”</hi> The “jubilee trumpets” (<hi type="italic">Eng</hi>. Ver. “trumpets of rams’ horns”) are the same as the “jubilee horn” (<hi type="italic">Eng</hi>. Ver. “rams’ horn”) in <reference osisRef="Josh.6.5">Jos 6:5</reference>, for which the abbreviated form <hi type="italic">shophar</hi> (trumpet, <reference osisRef="Josh.6.5">Jos 6:5</reference>; cf. <reference osisRef="Exod.19.16">Exo 19:16</reference>) or <hi type="italic">jobel</hi> (jubilee: <reference osisRef="Exod.19.13">Exo 19:13</reference>) is used. They were not the silver trumpets of the priests (Num 10:1.), but large horns, or instruments in the shape of a horn, which gave a loud far-sounding tone (see at <reference osisRef="Lev.23.24">Lev 23:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.25.11">Lev 25:11</reference>). For בש תּקע, blow the trumpet (<hi type="italic">lit</hi>. strike the trumpet), in <reference osisRef="Josh.6.4">Jos 6:4</reference>, בּקּרן משׁך, draw with the horn, i.e., blow the horn with long-drawn notes, is used in <reference osisRef="Josh.6.5">Jos 6:5</reference> (see at <reference osisRef="Exod.19.13">Exo 19:13</reference>). The people were then to go up, i.e., press into the town over the fallen wall; <hi type="italic">“every one straight before</hi> <hi type="italic">him,”</hi> i.e., every one was to go straight into the town without looking round at his neighbour either on the right hand or on the left (vid., <reference osisRef="Josh.6.20">Jos 6:20</reference>). <div eID="gen2720" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2721" type="x-p"/> Taking of Jericho. - In the account of this we have first of all a brief statement of the announcement of the divine message by Joshua to the priests and the people (<reference osisRef="Josh.6.6">Jos 6:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Josh.6.7">Jos 6:7</reference>); then the execution of the divine command (<reference osisRef="Josh.6.8-Josh.6.20">Jos 6:8-20</reference>); and lastly the burning of Jericho and deliverance of Rahab (<reference osisRef="Josh.6.21-Josh.6.27">Jos 6:21-27</reference>).
entries.6768287fb233fdeaedb2f1363aa37eb1c8e7c7f0: <reference osisRef="Josh.6.6-Josh.6.7">Jos 6:6-7</reference> <div eID="gen2721" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2722" type="x-p"/> In communicating the divine command with reference to the arrangements for taking Jericho, Joshua mentions in the first place merely the principal thing to be observed. The plural ויּאמרוּ (“they said”), in <reference osisRef="Josh.6.7">Jos 6:7</reference>, must not be altered, but is to be explained on the ground that Joshua did not make the proclamation to the people himself, but through the medium oft he shoterim, who were appointed to issue his commands (see <reference osisRef="Josh.1.10-Josh.1.11">Jos 1:10-11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.3.2-Josh.3.3">Jos 3:2-3</reference>). In this proclamation the more minute instructions concerning the order of march, which had been omitted in <reference osisRef="Josh.6.3-Josh.6.5">Jos 6:3-5</reference>, are given; namely, that החלוּץ was to march in front of the ark. By החלוּץ, <hi type="italic">“the equipped</hi> (or armed) <hi type="italic">man,”</hi> we are not to understand all the fighting men, as <hi type="italic">Knobel</hi> supposes; for in the description of the march which follows, the whole of the fighting men (“all the men of war,” <reference osisRef="Josh.6.3">Jos 6:3</reference>) are divided into החלוּץ and המּאסּף (<hi type="italic">Eng. Ver</hi>. “the armed men” and “the rereward,” <reference osisRef="Josh.6.9">Jos 6:9</reference> and <reference osisRef="Josh.6.13">Jos 6:13</reference>), so that the former can only have formed one division of the army. It is very natural therefore to suppose, as <hi type="italic">Kimchi</hi> and <hi type="italic">Rashi</hi> do, that the former were the fighting men of the tribes of Reuben, Gad, and half Manasseh (הצּבא חלוּצי, <reference osisRef="Josh.4.13">Jos 4:13</reference>), and the latter the fighting men of the rest of the tribes. On the meaning of מאסּף, see at Num 10:25. If we turn to the account of the facts themselves, we shall see at once, that in the report of the angel’s message, in <reference osisRef="Josh.6.3-Josh.6.5">Jos 6:3-5</reference>, several other points have been passed over for the purpose of avoiding too many repetitions, and have therefore to be gathered from the description of what actually occurred.
